cognate: Serbian zvezda / Lithuanian žvaigždė continue the Balto-Slavic star word (slab label kaikki:ǵʰwoysdʰeh₂); sestrica / sesulė are independently suffixed diminutives of the inherited sister word *swésōr.
drift_or_renewal: Different diminutive formations; Serbian also has a vocative sister address and specifies the traversing/morning star.
shared_syntax: Apposition identifying a star as sister; Serbian genitive sister + star under a single preposition, Lithuanian nominative star + sister. The other Serbian anchors show vocative apposition.
context: Both traditions assign kinship roles to heavenly bodies. Serbian adjacent context makes the moon a brother; Lithuanian context makes the sun a mother and a stellar group a brother. This recurring structured celestial family is more distinctive than juxtaposition of sky vocabulary. The witnesses are late collected songs: the defensible ancestral scope is a possible Balto-Slavic formula, not a demonstrated pan-Indo-European formula; independent personification and regional diffusion remain alternatives.
phrase: The star is a sister / star-sister.

cognate: Serbian nositi and Lithuanian nešti continue the carrying root *neḱ- (slab h₁neḱ-); ruka and ranka continue the same Balto-Slavic hand/arm noun (slab wrenk).
drift_or_renewal: Serbian iterative present plural versus Lithuanian prefixed past singular; Lithuanian adds white as an epithet. Ring words are not cognate.
shared_syntax: Bird subject + carry/bring + accusative hand, with a ring associated with that severed hand in the adjoining unit.
context: The Serbian wider context explicitly identifies two ravens and delivery to the mother. Lithuanian has the black raven returning with a white hand and gold ring. The severed hand plus identifying ring makes this a highly specific death-news motif, not ordinary carrying in the hands. This is a low-confidence inherited Balto-Slavic phraseological candidate: nineteenth-century song witnesses and possible diffusion of a migratory ballad motif prevent secure prehistoric dating.
phrase: The raven(s) carry back a hand with a ring.

Ottoman flag, shepherd simile, celestial reproach, Baltic moon’s military/horse imagery, and a Lithuanian prose tale title are not one inherited phrase.
